title: How Big of A Deal Are Psychedelic Medicines Likely to Be?
subtitle: We ask a meta-analysis and an AI Image generator.
text:
The Frontier Psychiatrists strives for a world where health-themed newsletter writing can be at once “funny” and “hip-hop-informed” in a way that makes health-related science more comprehensible. Today, we are trying something new. Yes, that is the royal We. Although We (Owen Muir, M.D., DFAACAP, unless otherwise noted) author this newsletter the old-fashioned way—with bespoke typos and spelling errors to indicate there is no AI Bot cranking out the remarkable amount of writing by any human standard on these digital pages…We are not about using an AI image generator to make a silly point.

Subscribe now

I have previously argued for the “Skee-Lo Standard” (using the Muir-Skee-Lo Emotionally Corrective Equation) in which Effect Size is converted into “height differences.” Effect Size (ES) is in units of standard deviations. The SD of the height of the American Male Human is 2.5 inches. Thus, the MS-L EQE takes the ES (sometimes reported as Standard Mean Difference or SMD) and multiplies it by 2.5, to create a relative height difference, as a standard way to understand the differences in things.

Skee-Lo, of course, is the 5’8” tall rapper who sang “I Wish”:

“I wish I was a little bit taller, I wish I was a baller”

Which struck me as a great way to standardize our understanding of the potency of medical treatments. There may be other hip-hop-inspired ways to share an understanding of “how big of a deal” a science finding is!

There has been a recent meta-analysis on psychedelic medicine, so I decided a “trippy article” was in order. How big of a deal are psychedelic medicines? As someone who recently senior authored 8 articles on the topic (with excellent commentary1 by Lynn Marie Morski, MD, ESQ., president of the Psychedelic Medicine Association) published in the American Journal of Therapeutics, I am excited for as many papers on the topic that will also have to cite my papers as possible.

A brief aside about meta-analysis—these are of course papers about published papers. This is both important research and, at the same time, easy to crank out. One of my favorite articles on the topic is2:

The Mass Production of Redundant, Misleading, and Conflicted Systematic Reviews and Meta-analyses

by the hilarious and remarkably adept Dr. Ioannidis. You know, the guy who also authored “Why Most Published Research Findings are False3”

With that “grain of salt” seasoning, I am thrilled to continue with my article presenting meta-analysis data from a reputable journal (psychiatry research) to you. Yao, et. al. did a meta-analysis4 of psychedelic treatments (not venturing into Ibogaine5 or Ketamine,6 ):

We aim to systematically review and meta-analyze the effectiveness and safety of psychedelics [psilocybin, ayahuasca (active component DMT), LSD and MDMA] in treating symptoms of various mental disorders. Web of Science, Embase, EBSCO, and PubMed were searched up to February 2024 and 126 articles were finally included.

Psilocybin, in their review, leads the pack, with the most published studies (N=28) and the biggest effect sizes in mood disorders:

Specifically, psilocybin (Hedges’ g = -1.49, 95% CI [-1.67, -1.30]) showed the strongest therapeutic effect among four psychedelics

Here, I’m going to attempt to visually represent the difference between psilocybin’s effect size, with the rapper on the left at 5’8” and the one on the right height adjusted using the Hedges g (a measure of ES) using the MS-L EQE, as plugged into DALL-E:

Prompt: “can you make a picture of two rappers, on 68" tall and the other 71.728" tall next to him”

I strongly suspect this is not accurate, in terms of proportions, but one is taller than the other. So, I’ll include it.

Ayahuasca is converted into DMT in our bodies, consumed as a ceremonial tea that includes an MAO inhibitor, and is reported to have the following effect size: (Hedges’ g = -1.34, 95% CI [-1.86, -0.82]).

I strongly suspect the “safety data” reviewed is inaccurate:

The most common adverse event with psychedelics was headache. Nearly a third of the articles reported that no participants reported lasting adverse effects.

Which is profoundly misleading. The following is a list of common effects of ayahuasca, which can last between 4- to-6 hours:

• nausea and vomiting (induced by drinking the decoction)

• diarrhoea

• euphoria

• feelings of connection and unity

• introspection

• intense visual and auditory hallucinations

• experiencing powerful emotions

• anxiety

• panic and fear

• moderate increase in blood pressure and heart rate

• increased body temperature.

In my world of medical research, those are all at least Treatment-Emergent Adverse Effects (TEAEs). It seems psychedelic researchers might do well to avail themselves of helpful fact sheets from the NIH, like this one.

The authors of this meta-analysis go on to cite the following additional data: MDMA (Hedges’ g = -0.83, 95% CI [-1.33, -0.32]), and LSD (Hedges’ g = -0.65, 95% CI [-1.03, -0.27]). The issue, of course, with any research, is thoroughness, and in this review, they don’t include the topline data from the largest and most well-controlled clinical trial of LSD to date, as performed by Dan Karlin M.D.’s team at Mind Med. You know, the one that demonstrates this (MM-120 is the proprietary name for the “mind med version” of LSD):

MM-120 100 µg significantly reduced HAM-A by 21.3 points, showing a 7.6 improvement from placebo to week 4 (P = .0004; Cohen’s d effect size = .88).

With a sample size of 198. When our team published a review, in the American Journal of Theraputics, the abstract noted that this is the largest study ever done:

Only one large-scale clinical trial (>50 participants) has been conducted on LSD in the contemporary era of psychedelic research. Further studies with large sample sizes are needed to explore potential clinical applications.7

This is not to dunk, overmuch, on colleagues getting a paper out. It is to say: any meta-analysis is only as good as its methodology and the methodology of the underlying papers. We should expect a storm of these reviews, meta-reviews, and network-meta-meta-meta analyses. They are easier than doing complex, highly-regulated, original research. I should know—I’m “guilty” of the same thing in my recent series of reviews! Good reviews get cited, and even not-so-good reviews will get cited, making the world of academic clout chasing go round and round.

Excellent trial design can’t be recreated by meta-analysis, they are different tools, not proxies for each other. Stay skeptical, friends. To my colleagues, consider spending more time on original research.
